objectives.name: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
Align solutions to business value pillars
Design system prompts, templates and guardrails
Apply zero-shot, few-shot and reasoning techniques
Optimize context windows and token usage
Implement caching, modular prompts and Skills
Match retrieval to data shape and queries
Select MCP, API/CLI or agent-to-agent mechanisms
Evaluate progressive discovery versus monolithic context
Define accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security metrics
Design datasets and mixed-method test frameworks
Conduct A/B tests and iterative improvements
Diagnose prompt failure, hallucinations and model mismatch
Monitor performance with logs and observability
Identify risks, limitations and failure modes
Support discovery, design, handoff, monitoring and iteration
Configure Claude tools and environments for teams

questions.title: Choose a first investment under uncertain demand
questions.stem: Only 8% of association members use its well-maintained search portal. Staff do not know whether members need better search or rarely need it. One discovery cycle remains before architecture approval. What should happen FIRST?

options.text: Estimate savings from membership counts and select the cheapest architecture producing cited technical answers.
options.why: Membership count does not establish actual workload.

options.text: Survey requested assistant features and prioritize them before evaluating how members currently resolve questions.
options.why: Feature preference is weaker than observed unmet need.

options.text: Benchmark multi-agent answer quality against search and extrapolate adoption from the measured quality difference.
options.why: Answer quality alone does not establish unmet demand.

options.text: Observe question journeys; separate demand from search failure and define testable adoption and resolution goals.
options.why: This establishes demand and the actual failure boundary.

questions.decision: Validate whether a meaningful unmet job exists before committing to a sophisticated solution; low portal use is not itself a diagnosis.

questions.title: The transaction boundary for a reversible draft
questions.stem: Curators accept AI-drafted exhibition labels, but publication also requires accessibility review and an image license. The design treats draft acceptance as publication approval. Which TWO changes preserve these gates and a recoverable visitor-visible record?

options.text: Infer license approval from the curator's accepted edits before activating the exhibition label.
options.why: Free-text inference cannot establish the required gate.

options.text: Publish to a small visitor segment and substitute feedback for accessibility review.
options.why: Visitor sampling does not satisfy existing approval obligations.

options.text: Gate activation on separate accessibility and license approvals after draft acceptance.
options.why: This preserves the actual publication authority boundary.

options.text: Check accessibility during first drafting and inherit the result after wording changes.
options.why: Changed published content may invalidate prior checks.

options.text: Store each activated label with its evidence, approval versions and the links needed for rollback.
options.why: This makes published state reproducible and recoverable.

questions.decision: The useful AI boundary is drafting; publication is a separately governed transition with versioned gates and historical state.

questions.title: An agent is justified by the unresolved path
questions.stem: Vendor investigations may end after one lookup or uncover indirect relationships requiring more research. Fixed workflows stop too early. Analysts own final findings, and expenditure is capped. Which design best fits?

options.text: Run agents through predefined entity-category checklists and merge when all finish.
options.why: Fixed categories may still miss newly discovered relation types.

options.text: Use a larger one-shot model to identify cited relationships from the initial record for analysts.
options.why: Initial data cannot establish unqueried relationships.

options.text: Add fixed registry stages for indirect relationships and run every stage on every case.
options.why: Fixed stages remain insensitive to discovered branching needs.

options.text: Use a budgeted agent with approved tools, unresolved-branch reports and analyst review.
options.why: Dynamic steps match unpredictable relationship discovery.

questions.decision: Choose adaptive evidence gathering because the next step depends on discoveries; preserve explicit spend and final decision boundaries.

questions.title: When specialists share a scarce budget
questions.stem: Habitat, taxonomy and permit workers repeatedly buy identical datasets, exhausting a shared query budget before conflicts are resolved. Evidence and dissent must survive synthesis. Which TWO changes best support parallel research?

options.text: Retain structured findings and dissent; reserve budget for coordinator-led conflict resolution.
options.why: This preserves dissent and funds the synthesis need.

options.text: Share query budgets and an evidence registry centrally so workers can reuse approved results.
options.why: This prevents duplicate spending while retaining parallel work.

options.text: Give equal independent budgets and merge by majority when any worker exhausts its allocation.
options.why: Separate caps do not prevent duplicate spending or resolve dissent.

options.text: Let workers trade budget through shared chat and judge coordination from the final narrative.
options.why: Informal negotiation lacks an enforceable shared resource contract.

options.text: Run permits last to inspect purchased datasets and choose the best-supported overall conclusion.
options.why: Serial legal review does not fix duplicate acquisition.

questions.decision: Parallel work still needs shared resource arbitration and a funded synthesis contract; independent budgets can waste common resources.

questions.title: A dependency test before parallelizing
questions.stem: Clause validation must precede obligation extraction. A negotiation brief needs those obligations and an independent, read-only market lookup. Which change reduces latency without breaking evidence dependencies?

options.text: Look up market data alongside clause validation; keep later stages behind their inputs.
options.why: This parallelizes an independent branch while respecting dependencies.

options.text: Keep the whole analysis serial because obligations and the brief depend on earlier evidence.
options.why: Independent market lookup can still run concurrently.

options.text: Use three independent brief writers and replace clause validation with agreement.
options.why: Agreement does not validate missing clause boundaries.

options.text: Extract obligations from partial clauses and revise the brief as missing clauses arrive.
options.why: Speculative dependencies risk incomplete consequential analysis.

questions.decision: Decompose and parallelize according to the evidence dependency graph, not the number of model calls.

questions.title: A capacity commitment with a rework ceiling
questions.stem: Use the exhibit. Corrections and recurring evaluation both consume editor capacity. What is the maximum assisted-case correction rate that still releases 600 net hours monthly, stated to one decimal without overstating the ceiling?

options.text: 6.7% of assisted cases, including correction and evaluation workload.
options.why: This unnecessarily leaves more than 180 released hours above the target; it is not the maximum supported correction rate.

options.text: 25.0% of assisted cases, excluding recurring evaluation workload.
options.why: This omits the recurring eighty-hour capacity cost.

options.text: 19.4% of assisted cases, including correction and evaluation workload.
63.8% of assisted cases, applying savings to every monthly abstract.
options.why: This assumes universal adoption rather than sixty percent.

questions.decision: Assisted baseline saving is 960 hours; correction consumes 1,440r hours and evaluation consumes 80. Solve the actual capacity commitment before promising it.

questions.title: Design a productive disagreement
questions.stem: Two literature workers repeat one study, while a methodology worker finds a decisive confound. The coordinator reports the majority verdict. Which THREE requirements best support diverse evidence for scientists' final review?

options.text: Use a synthesis rubric that weighs decisive constraints and leaves unresolved evidence visible.
options.why: Evidence quality should determine synthesis.

options.text: Give workers the emerging majority verdict so research can support the likely conclusion.
options.why: This encourages correlated confirmation bias.

options.text: Require each domain to return objections and citations in typed outputs, preserving material dissent.
options.why: This prevents dissent from disappearing in aggregation.

options.text: Track source dependence so repeated studies do not count as independent support.
options.why: Two workers can repeat one evidence source.

options.text: Add literature workers to stabilize the majority despite differences in retrieved papers.
options.why: More correlated votes do not resolve confounding.

questions.decision: Multi-agent diversity requires independent evidence and explicit dissent handling; the number of agreeing agents is not a scientific confidence measure.

questions.title: Known checklist, uncertain language
questions.stem: A fixed filing workflow extracts 12 fields, applies published checks and drafts a cover note, escalating exceptions. It covers the pilot workload; an agent adds loops without quality gains. Which architecture best fits the approved release?

options.text: Choose the agent now so adaptive planning can accommodate possible future filing changes.
options.why: Possible future needs do not justify current overhead.

options.text: Use the fixed workflow with explicit exception handling and modular interfaces for approved changes.
options.why: This meets current needs without unproven orchestration cost.

options.text: Combine extraction and drafting in one model call, using officer review instead of rule checks.
options.why: This discards useful deterministic validation.

options.text: Run both designs on every filing and select whichever produces the more complete explanation.
options.why: Explanation completeness does not justify duplicate work.

questions.decision: Predictable tasks support explicit workflows; preserve modularity without paying for autonomy that has no demonstrated benefit.

questions.title: An architecture for revocable derived knowledge
questions.stem: Article licenses can expire during research. Access is checked only at session start, and retained passages are reused indefinitely. Expired material must not support new answers. Which design best preserves useful ongoing research?

options.text: Refresh login tokens regularly and retain previously retrieved passages until the session ends.
options.why: Token refresh does not preserve expired article rights.

options.text: Delete the complete conversation after any license expires and ask users to reconstruct research.
options.why: This unnecessarily destroys unaffected authorized state.

options.text: Track evidence rights, recheck use and rebuild affected findings from still-authorized material.
options.why: This scopes invalidation while preserving authorized work.

options.text: Suppress expired citations while continuing to generate from their saved summaries.
options.why: Uncited use can still violate the stated restriction.

questions.decision: Authorization and lineage must travel with derived evidence; selective invalidation preserves useful state while respecting changed rights.

questions.title: Select a pilot around feasible evidence
questions.stem: An archive needs a useful, measurable six-week pilot. Experts can label handwritten-search relevance; attribution lacks consensus, and itinerary ticketing integration is unavailable this quarter. Which TWO commitments best fit?

options.text: Agree success measures, uncertainty and who owns decision gates before expanding into interpretation or ticketing.
options.why: This bounds claims and expansion decisions.

options.text: Prioritize historical attribution because transformation value outweighs unresolved labels within six weeks.
options.why: Potential value does not provide feasible pilot evidence.

options.text: Pilot handwriting discovery with expert relevance labels and user tasks; keep attribution separate.
options.why: This chooses a feasible outcome and evaluation path.

options.text: Build a common agent framework for all projects, deferring selection until integrations become available.
options.why: This delays the measurable pilot decision.

options.text: Demonstrate invented ticket availability and use visitor enthusiasm as evidence the itinerary is ready.
options.why: Demonstrations cannot establish an operational integrated outcome.

questions.decision: Choose a useful hypothesis that can be implemented and evaluated within the actual decision window.

questions.title: A service tier needs worst-slice evidence
questions.stem: Release requires accuracy ≥95% separately on digital and scanned forms, plus p95 ≤3 seconds. All candidates pass access checks. Minimize cost only among eligible candidates. Which exhibit candidate should be selected?

options.text: Willow: lower cost, covering scan deficits through confidence-based routing not yet evaluated.
options.why: Unevaluated routing cannot establish current gate compliance.

options.text: Reed: strongest weighted average and more budget left for scan tuning.
options.why: A global average cannot override the scan gate.

options.text: Flint: both accuracy gates and latency pass at the lowest feasible cost.
options.why: Flint is the only candidate passing every gate.

options.text: Slate: strongest scan accuracy outweighs its modest latency overrun.
options.why: Slate fails the contracted completion gate.

questions.decision: Independent slice gates prevent a dominant easy workload from hiding failure in a supported difficult slice.

questions.title: Model choice after a distribution shift
questions.stem: A sorter selected for short English descriptions misroutes a new cohort's long, mixed-language records with measurements. The old cohort still performs well; a costlier model improves measurement extraction. What should guide the next selection?

options.text: Replace the original model globally because it improves measurement extraction on the new cohort.
options.why: New-slice improvement does not establish global value.

options.text: Route on self-reported confidence and assume escalation works until production disproves it.
options.why: Routing quality is an unvalidated assumption.

options.text: Keep the model and exclude mixed-language records from quality metrics as unsupported outliers.
options.why: Supported scope cannot be changed silently.

options.text: Test both cohorts and validated routing against new quality, cost and latency requirements.
options.why: This tests the changed workload and retained behavior.

questions.decision: Revisit selection with the actual supported distribution, measuring the complete system and preserved baseline.

questions.title: A testable abstention contract
questions.stem: A troubleshooting assistant guesses firmware when logs omit it, although the same error code has different meanings across firmware families. Which TWO prompt changes best define safe, testable recommendations for staff review?

options.text: Load every firmware manual and choose whichever family most resembles the reported error code.
options.why: More manuals do not establish the missing device version.

options.text: Require evidence for the firmware version; ask for clarification or escalate when it is missing.
options.why: This defines the missing-evidence decision boundary.

options.text: Request longer explanations of troubleshooting steps so staff can identify guessed firmware versions.
options.why: Explanation length does not prevent unsupported recommendations.

options.text: Show contrasting firmware examples and structure the evidence, uncertainty and permitted next steps for review.
options.why: This makes the desired distinction testable.

options.text: Accept a consistent firmware estimate and use high model confidence as sufficient version evidence.
options.why: Internal confidence cannot supply missing firmware evidence.

questions.decision: A prompt should define what evidence permits action advice and what happens when it is absent; examples target that boundary.

questions.title: Teach a rule without leaking the answer
questions.stem: A classifier confuses proposed and enacted rules. Development examples contain only simple enacted cases. Experts can annotate six more; a separate release holdout exists. Which example design best targets confusion while preserving independent evaluation?

options.text: Add six enacted cases with longer explanations and unchanged status instructions.
options.why: More enacted cases miss the confused distinction.

options.text: Contrast rule statuses in labeled development cases; test untouched release documents.
options.why: Contrastive examples teach the actual status boundary.

options.text: Move difficult holdout cases into the prompt and report gains on that same holdout.
options.why: This contaminates the claimed independent evaluation.

options.text: Show unlabeled proposed rules and infer status by resemblance to enacted examples.
options.why: This does not provide authoritative boundary supervision.

questions.decision: Few-shot examples should expose the contested distinction; release cases must remain independent of prompt construction.

questions.title: Context for a changing analytical hypothesis
questions.stem: A vibration investigation's compressed history treats an early hypothesis as confirmed and loses its later rejection. Context can hold structured state and selected evidence, but not full history. Which strategy best preserves changing interpretations?

options.text: Track facts, active and rejected hypotheses separately, with dated evidence and on-demand extracts.
options.why: This preserves epistemic status under compaction.

options.text: Keep one narrative of the most-mentioned explanation and append the latest sensor extract.
options.why: Frequency can promote a rejected hypothesis.

options.text: Retain every raw sensor extract and remove analyst messages first as less objective context.
options.why: Analyst decisions and hypothesis status are lost.

options.text: Reconstruct earlier reasoning from the current answer and adopt it as the next session's state.
options.why: Reconstruction is not a source-backed state record.

questions.decision: Compaction must preserve the status of claims, not merely their wording; durable state distinguishes observation from hypothesis.

questions.title: A shared prefix with changing procedure versions
questions.stem: Procurement requests share common policy but usually need only one specialist procedure. Tax, delivery and sustainability procedures have different owners and release schedules. Which TWO reuse choices reduce context while preserving version accountability?

options.text: Cache changing supplier profiles before shared policy to improve organization-wide prefix reuse.
options.why: Dynamic leading content fragments shared-prefix reuse.

options.text: Combine procedures in one prompt and infer which versions were used from final answer wording.
options.why: This weakens explicit procedure version accountability.

options.text: Load relevant versioned Skills from their applicability metadata and record which procedure was used.
options.why: This reduces unused procedures while preserving lineage.

options.text: Keep policy in a stable prefix; log its version and measured cache writes and reads.
options.why: This preserves measurable common-policy reuse.

options.text: Store procedure names only and use general knowledge unless a user requests a specific version.
options.why: The model still needs authoritative procedural instructions.

questions.decision: Common policy and task-specific procedures have different reuse and ownership boundaries; version both and measure actual cache behavior.

questions.title: A model upgrade changes the failure mix
questions.stem: A new correspondence model improves critical reasoning but sometimes breaks the schema and produces longer answers. The old model passes schema/latency gates but misses that reasoning slice. Prompt and output controls can change. What experiment best supports selection?

options.text: Deploy the new model for reasoning quality and tune schema and answer length using production feedback.
options.why: Known release failures remain unresolved.

options.text: Select the cheaper token configuration and rely on reviewers to absorb reasoning and schema differences.
options.why: Cost does not establish the independent quality gates.

options.text: Keep the old model because schema compliance proves its failures are easier to manage operationally.
options.why: The critical reasoning gate still fails.

options.text: Test each complete setup against the same gates for reasoning cases, schema, completion time and total cost.
options.why: This compares feasible complete configurations.

questions.decision: Configuration selection must resolve the complete gate set; a model upgrade is not an automatic quality or operational upgrade.

questions.title: A reusable Skill is still an input boundary
questions.stem: A reusable document-analysis Skill includes a script that accepts arbitrary output paths and inserts spreadsheet cells into shell commands. External spreadsheets are common. Which THREE requirements should precede routine use?

options.text: Limit what the runtime can access and test malicious files alongside the ordinary workflows.
options.why: Reusable procedures still need bounded capabilities and testing.

options.text: Rely on the Skill's prohibition of unsafe commands when scripts interpret inputs.
options.why: Instructions do not repair unsafe argument handling.

options.text: Review and version the instructions and executable resources together; record which release was loaded.
options.why: Executable resources belong to the reviewed artifact.

options.text: Cache the executable script in the shared prompt and rely on its first-request validation.
options.why: Caching does not validate changed untrusted input.

options.text: Validate arguments and output paths; treat spreadsheet cells as untrusted data.
options.why: This enforces the concrete execution trust boundary.

questions.decision: Procedural reuse does not make executable content or external data trusted; validate inputs and bound execution for every relevant use.

questions.title: Instruction precedence with a legitimate conflict
questions.stem: An uploaded old manual explains an existing installation but instructs recommending a discontinued accessory. Trusted policy permits only supported recommendations. Which response best serves the historical question within that policy?

options.text: Discard the manual entirely and explain the installation using general current product knowledge.
options.why: The policy permits useful historical explanation.

options.text: Recommend the compatible accessory with a disclaimer explaining its discontinued support status.
options.why: A disclaimer does not satisfy the recommendation boundary.

options.text: Have the user accept unsupported advice as permission to override the supported-device restriction.
options.why: User consent cannot change the trusted service boundary.

options.text: Explain the historical specifications and support status; keep current recommendations within the policy.
options.why: This preserves evidence without importing old instructions.

questions.decision: Distinguish discussing historical evidence from adopting its instructions or making a prohibited current recommendation.

questions.title: Capability bloat is an ownership problem too
questions.stem: HR, finance and procurement tools have overlapping names but different authority and effects. The assistant often chooses writes when users want explanations. What should change FIRST before catalogue optimization?

options.text: Merge similar endpoints and let a natural-language mode determine whether to read or write.
options.why: A vague mode preserves consequential ambiguity.

options.text: Clarify tool names and distinguish read/write intent, authority and effects; test selection.
options.why: This clarifies the consequential selection boundary.

options.text: Assign a larger model to selection while keeping the overlapping names and effect descriptions.
options.why: Model size does not repair the interface contract.

options.text: Defer every tool and load the three shortest matching descriptions to reduce catalogue competition.
options.why: Shortness does not establish semantic suitability.

questions.decision: Clarify intent and authority before reducing catalog size; apparently similar capabilities can have materially different effects.

questions.title: Session identity is not object permission
questions.stem: A document MCP server verifies identity and audience, but its shared account returns Matter B documents to a Matter A user. Logging happens after content enters context. Which TWO controls directly enforce access boundaries?

options.text: Redact titles in audit logs but retain content access because identity and audience checks passed.
options.why: Identity and token audience do not establish object rights.

options.text: Check that the user currently has access to the matter before returning documents or search results.
options.why: This closes object-level access before disclosure.

options.text: Have users confirm a document belongs to their matter before the shared account fetches it.
options.why: Untrusted confirmation cannot establish backend authorization.

options.text: Enforce delegated rights in the server and require cross-matter denial and revocation tests before release.
options.why: This prevents backend privilege from expanding delegated rights.

options.text: Put the user's matter ID in the prompt and ask the assistant to reject mismatching documents.
options.why: The content has already crossed the boundary.

questions.decision: Authenticate the user and token correctly, then separately authorize each resource and action before content leaves the server.

questions.title: Streaming does not erase the commit tail
questions.stem: A new assistant streams sooner but finishes later because tool retries increase. The SLA requires a validated recommendation within four seconds, including citation checks and an authorization-sensitive tool. How should the configuration be assessed?

options.text: Accept earlier streaming and complete citation checks after marking the recommendation ready.
options.why: The final recommendation would not yet be validated.

options.text: Measure validated completion tails and retry delays, and report time to the first token separately.
options.why: This preserves the actual acceptance metric.

options.text: Measure generation alone because the integration team owns the tool-retry behavior.
options.why: The contractual service includes the tool path.

options.text: Subtract average retry time from completion p95 to assess the remaining model contribution.
options.why: Adjusted marginal metrics do not establish user completion.

questions.decision: Perceived responsiveness and usable completion are separate measures; streaming does not satisfy validation or authorization dependencies.

questions.title: Diagnose the unsampled customer
questions.stem: Uniform 1% trace sampling mostly captures large tenants. A small regulated tenant reports timeouts despite healthy global averages. Sampling precedes tenant/region metadata, and content retention is limited. Which TWO changes best improve diagnosis?

options.text: Exclude small tenants until their traffic yields statistics as stable as large-tenant dashboards.
options.why: This conceals supported-user failures.

options.text: Double uniform sampling and use the larger global sample as the primary health measure.
options.why: A larger skewed sample may still miss the tenant.

options.text: Capture complete prompts indefinitely so small tenants eventually have enough trace examples.
options.why: This violates the stated data limit.

options.text: Track required slices' failures and tails, with owners and bounded redacted incident evidence.
options.why: This connects diagnosis to contractual slices and action.

options.text: Correlate permitted metadata; sample underrepresented slices and failures deliberately.
options.why: This makes low-volume failures observable.

questions.decision: Observability sampling must support the service's actual slices and failure modes; global averages cannot diagnose an unsampled tenant.

questions.title: A chunking boundary around a definition
questions.stem: A standards assistant cites the correct requirement but misinterprets a term defined in a separate glossary. Paragraph chunks preserve headings but omit definition links. Which evidence-pipeline change best addresses this?

options.text: Keep requirement chunks unchanged and have the larger generator supply definitions from its technical knowledge.
options.why: General knowledge may conflict with the standard's definition.

options.text: Double paragraph overlap, expecting nearby context to provide glossary definitions often enough.
options.why: The glossary is separately located.

options.text: Retrieve each requirement with its linked definition from the same version, then test term-dependent questions.
options.why: This supplies the authoritative meaning of the term.

options.text: Replace specialized terms with everyday synonyms so meanings become inferable from context.
options.why: Synonyms can change the standard's defined meaning.

questions.decision: Correct section retrieval is insufficient when authoritative semantics live in linked evidence; preserve and retrieve those relationships.

questions.title: Retrieval for aggregates rather than snippets
questions.stem: A finance assistant sums top-retrieved invoice summaries for quarterly unpaid balances. Exact totals, approved status and row permissions matter; the database is authoritative. Which integration best supports aggregates while retaining policy RAG?

options.text: Increase top-k until the total stabilizes and cite retrieved summaries as complete.
options.why: Stability does not establish complete result coverage.

options.text: Embed quarterly summaries and reuse their balance totals until the next index refresh.
options.why: A static summary can be stale and permission-inappropriate.

options.text: Have two models sum the same retrieved invoices and accept totals within a small tolerance.
options.why: Agreement cannot fix missing rows or authorization.

options.text: Run authorized complete aggregates with record lineage; keep RAG for policy explanations.
options.why: Structured aggregation supplies complete exact scoped results.

questions.decision: Match query semantics to the data shape; exact permission-scoped aggregates need authoritative structured computation.

questions.title: A local integration with a narrow purpose
questions.stem: A local assistant needs an existing deterministic validation CLI for a checked-out dataset. It returns structured results and uses controlled temporary storage. No remote discovery or agent coordination is needed. Which TWO choices best fit?

options.text: Have local agents negotiate each validation rule so the assistant can adapt the CLI's established checks.
options.why: Negotiation is unnecessary and changes the check contract.

options.text: Replace the CLI with model judgments on sampled rows, returning natural-language validation findings.
options.why: This discards authoritative deterministic validation.

options.text: Deploy a remote server exposing broad local filesystem operations for future assistant workflows.
options.why: This adds unnecessary infrastructure and broad capability.

options.text: Record CLI, dataset and result versions; test failures and timeouts before adding infrastructure.
options.why: This makes the local integration reproducible and robust.

options.text: Wrap the CLI with typed arguments, path limits and explicit exit-status handling.
options.why: This uses the sufficient existing local contract.

questions.decision: Protocol standardization is not itself a requirement; use the smallest reliable interface that meets the actual local task.

questions.title: Discovery cost where the core is large
questions.stem: A report needs 35 of 40 tools almost every run. Deferral saves initial tokens but adds repeated searches and schema loading; rare-task quality is unchanged. The deadline measures completed reports. Which configuration best fits?

options.text: Remove rare tools and treat lost rare-task support as an acceptable cost of faster reports.
options.why: Rare legitimate capabilities remain required.

options.text: Defer all tools because smaller initial context guarantees lower completion latency.
options.why: Discovery overhead can exceed the initial benefit.

options.text: Load common reporting tools directly; defer rare tools and measure complete reports.
options.why: This matches loading strategy to actual use frequency.

options.text: Keep deferred loading and make more searches so smaller schema groups arrive throughout reporting.
options.why: More searches do not address the demonstrated overhead.

questions.decision: Progressive loading is workload-dependent; compare total context and critical-path discovery cost for the actual task profile.

questions.title: A delegation chain without a confused deputy
questions.stem: An MCP research server uses its publisher subscription but grants licensed content to all authenticated callers, including public-only clients. Publisher calls must not receive the incoming research token. Which THREE requirements best preserve both boundaries?

options.text: Validate the research token and establish caller entitlements before licensed retrieval.
options.why: This combines correct audience with resource rights.

options.text: Treat the server subscription as authority for every authenticated caller, labeling licensed citations.
options.why: A citation label does not grant caller entitlement.

options.text: Use publisher credentials or a suitable exchange under contract, without forwarding the incoming bearer.
options.why: This prevents token audience passthrough.

options.text: Check caller rights on results and saved evidence; test public-only access to licensed material.
options.why: This prevents the service subscription becoming universal authority.

options.text: Let the model select public/licensed material from user wording while backend access stays unrestricted.
options.why: Untrusted wording cannot establish entitlement.

questions.decision: A privileged intermediary must preserve caller entitlements and separate resource-specific tokens; authentication is not universal subscription access.

questions.title: Retrieve the authoritative amendment
questions.stem: A named contract says 30 days, a signed amendment says 60, and an unsigned draft proposes 90. Retrieval finds all three. Signature status and effective dates are available. Which policy best establishes the current term?

options.text: Treat the original signed contract as controlling; amendments are supplementary.
options.why: An effective signed amendment can supersede it.

options.text: Average the conflicting terms and label them approximate pending a reviewer's contract interpretation.
options.why: Terms are not numerical estimates to average.

options.text: Filter applicable executed documents, resolve effective-date precedence and cite controlling terms.
options.why: This selects applicable authoritative evidence.

options.text: Use the newest upload's payment term and disclose its timestamp for transparency.
options.why: Upload recency does not establish execution or effect.

questions.decision: Evidence authority requires document identity, execution and effect, not semantic similarity or upload order.

questions.title: A gate between retrieval and reranking
questions.stem: Retrieval sends full candidate records to an external reranker before authorization filtering. Final answers contain permitted records only, but unauthorized content must not leave storage. Which change best retains useful reranking?

options.text: Remove reranking and retrieve one candidate, reducing the chance unauthorized content leaves storage.
options.why: Fewer candidates do not enforce authorization.

options.text: Keep the pipeline and redact forbidden citations when formatting the final user-visible answer.
options.why: Unauthorized content has already left storage.

options.text: Check authorization before reranking, then test relevance and completion tails using only permitted candidates.
options.why: This enforces the boundary before disclosure.

options.text: Keep reranking first, then delete forbidden records while retaining scores for the authorized final answer.
options.why: Deletion afterward cannot prevent the prohibited transfer.

questions.decision: Place enforcement before the trust boundary crossing; a correct final answer does not excuse unauthorized intermediate processing.

questions.title: Catalog discovery versus capability entitlement
questions.stem: Tool search exposes optional paid modules, but execution checks only argument schemas. Unlicensed operations must not run; users still need a discoverable upgrade path. Which TWO controls are required even if search hides unavailable tools?

options.text: Delete optional modules permanently and manually add paid features to each eligible conversation.
options.why: This removes legitimate discoverability rather than enforcing rights.

options.text: Put licensing rules in the system prompt and execute all schema-valid calls to handle ambiguity.
options.why: Prompt compliance does not enforce licensing.

options.text: Check tenant and user rights on each execution; test discovered but unlicensed tools.
options.why: Discovery does not establish execution authority.

options.text: Treat tool discovery as authorization because search already decides which capability fits the request.
options.why: Relevance selection is not entitlement verification.

options.text: Distinguish descriptions from availability; return a controlled unsupported or upgrade response.
options.why: This preserves clear product behavior without unauthorized execution.

questions.decision: What can be described or discovered is separate from what a tenant and principal may execute.

questions.title: Success needs a denominator
questions.stem: A translator reports 98% quality on completed outputs but excludes its new 12% refusal rate on difficult documents. The contract requires quality and supported-document coverage. Which evaluation best compares releases?

options.text: Exclude abstentions from service-quality metrics because they contain no translated output to judge.
options.why: This hides supported-workload coverage loss.

options.text: Report completion rates for eligible requests, quality on attempts and which refusals are justified.
options.why: This exposes the coverage-quality trade-off.

options.text: Count all refusals correct because avoiding uncertain translations is safer than attempting them.
options.why: Unjustified refusals still fail the supported service.

options.text: Compare easy common documents and extrapolate their quality across the remaining supported workload.
options.why: This excludes the changed difficult slice.

questions.decision: Use denominators aligned to the supported service; distinguish safe abstention from avoidable loss of coverage.

questions.title: An evaluation harness with changing state
questions.stem: Inventory-agent trials share a mutable database. Earlier trials consume stock, causing later identical requests to fail. Release requires correct plans and safe state changes from known inventory. Which TWO harness changes come first?

options.text: Have judges approve plausible explanations of inventory changes in failed transcripts.
options.why: Plausibility cannot establish the intended environment state.

options.text: Isolate state per trial and record its starting conditions, seed and configuration.
options.why: This removes unintended cross-trial state contamination.

options.text: Randomize order more often and treat average outcomes as removing stock depletion.
options.why: Order randomization does not restore intended initial conditions.

options.text: Increase temperature to explore alternatives after earlier trials consume stock.
options.why: This changes behavior without fixing the harness.

options.text: Check inventory and plan constraints in code; calibrate review of qualitative aspects.
options.why: This measures outcomes with appropriate graders.

questions.decision: Evaluate the agent and harness together, but control unintended environmental differences before attributing failures to the model.

questions.title: A/B evidence when treatment uptake differs
questions.stem: Technicians are randomized to two interfaces. Users select the new assistant less for hard cases but report faster handling when they use it. Leadership needs the effect of offering access. Which analysis best fits?

options.text: Compare only cases where technicians used their assigned assistant.
options.why: Selection on use can confound difficulty.

options.text: Compare eligible work by assigned arm; report uptake and case mix separately.
options.why: Assignment comparison preserves the intervention decision.

options.text: Extrapolate satisfied new-interface users' time gains to everyone offered access.
options.why: Satisfied users are a selected subset.

options.text: Move difficult unused cases into the old-interface group to balance completed interactions.
options.why: Post-assignment reassignment breaks the randomized comparison.

questions.decision: The decision concerns offering an interface; uptake is part of that intervention, not a reason to discard nonuse from its primary evaluation.

questions.title: Wrong answer despite correct retrieved evidence
questions.stem: Use the diagnostic exhibit. The same evidence yields a correct answer with a short prompt but a wrong one with an outdated production example. Model and retrieval are unchanged. What intervention is most justified?

options.text: Correct the example; retest unseen relationships and previously successful cases.
options.why: This tests the isolated prompt-level cause.

options.text: Double retrieved context so correct evidence appears more often than the conflicting example.
options.why: This masks rather than fixes conflicting instructions.

options.text: Upgrade the model while keeping the outdated example to test stronger reasoning under contradiction.
options.why: The known contradiction remains unnecessary.

options.text: Rebuild embeddings because a wrong answer implies poor retrieval alignment.
options.why: The relevant correct passage is already present.

questions.decision: Isolation points to a conflicting prompt example; repair the demonstrated boundary and test regressions before replacing unrelated components.

rows: Retrieved passage alone with short prompt

questions.title: Optimize the whole task, not calls alone
questions.stem: A smaller model cuts per-call cost 35% but increases retries, paid specialist review and completion tails. Successful outputs pass minimum textual quality. Which TWO measurements are needed before claiming a cheaper, preferable service?

options.text: Compare token prices alone because specialist review is charged outside the model team's budget.
options.why: Organizational billing does not remove total cost.

options.text: Exclude escalations to prevent human judgment from distorting the comparison of AI configurations.
options.why: Escalations are a consequence of the configuration.

options.text: Use successful-output quality as the sole gate because both models already pass textual accuracy.
options.why: This excludes coverage, cost and latency effects.

options.text: Check completion tails and escalation rates by critical slice against service gates.
options.why: This captures operational effects beyond successful model calls.

options.text: Compare cost per resolved case across equal workloads, including failures, retries and review.
options.why: This uses the economically relevant complete task.

questions.decision: Unit economics belong to a successfully completed supported task; retries and human review can reverse per-call savings.

questions.title: A logging change breaks reproducibility
questions.stem: Quality drops after concurrent releases. Logs retain IDs and answers but no longer record prompt/retrieval versions, preventing reproduction. Content retention must remain limited. Which repair best supports attribution?

options.text: Roll back every recent release and attribute any recovery to the newest model.
options.why: Multiple rollback changes cannot identify one cause.

options.text: Link outcomes to prompt and retrieval versions and release lineage; keep approved redacted samples.
options.why: This supplies reproducible context with bounded content.

options.text: Retain transcripts permanently because request IDs and metadata cannot explain semantic failures.
options.why: Permanent transcripts are not required to restore lineage.

options.text: Increase latency detail so execution timings can substitute for the missing configuration versions.
options.why: Latency detail cannot reconstruct absent version lineage.

questions.decision: Keep the minimal lineage needed to reproduce behavior; privacy-aware observability can retain useful metadata without blanket transcript storage.

questions.title: A judge should not prefer its own style
questions.stem: A judge rewards long answers, including unsupported repetition. Experts prefer concise, grounded answers; the rubric asks only for comprehensiveness. Which TWO changes best repair scalable grading while retaining human calibration?

options.text: Use two judges with the same rubric and average rankings, assuming agreement cancels length preference.
options.why: Shared rubric bias can persist across judges.

options.text: Test length against correctness independently; track judge versions and blinded expert checks.
options.why: This measures bias and calibration over time.

options.text: Rewrite responses into the judge's preferred style, leaving their claims unchanged.
options.why: This optimizes appearance rather than correctness.

options.text: Use expert-reviewed disagreements to calibrate criteria for evidence, unsupported claims and coverage.
options.why: This replaces stylistic preference with relevant criteria.

options.text: Cap length and treat shorter answers as equally correct while retaining the comprehensiveness rubric.
options.why: Length limits do not establish factual correctness.

questions.decision: Rubric quality and calibration determine grading validity; multiple uncalibrated judges cannot rescue the wrong criterion.

questions.title: A retrieval refresh changes who is supported
questions.stem: After a source refresh, global groundedness rises but a small region gets wrong effective dates. Tests now follow headquarters-heavy index proportions rather than supported users. Model and prompts are unchanged. What should diagnosis do FIRST?

options.text: Test regional user slices; inspect coverage and date metadata against authoritative sources.
options.why: This tests changed evidence coverage and evaluation weighting.

options.text: Have regional users adopt headquarters terminology so retrieval finds dominant-index evidence.
options.why: This avoids the supported regional requirement.

options.text: Increase reasoning budget to address temporal inference across all requests.
options.why: Missing or misweighted evidence is a more direct cause.

options.text: Accept the gain because index proportions provide representative evaluation sampling.
options.why: Index composition is not the supported user distribution.

questions.decision: An index-weighted average can improve while supported-user quality worsens; diagnose evidence and sampling at the affected slice.

questions.title: An operational gate for sustained quality
questions.stem: A revenue assistant must keep monthly reports accurate while schemas and business definitions change independently. Monitoring covers only uptime and spend; semantic-drift ownership is unclear. Which THREE additions best support handoff?

options.text: Define repair, regression and rollback procedures that retain the last validated setup on gate failure.
options.why: This connects detection to safe iteration.

options.text: Automatically reprompt on every source change and treat speed of adaptation as correctness evidence.
options.why: Automatic adaptation still requires validation.

options.text: Use uptime as the quality proxy because available sources underpin accurate reports.
options.why: Necessary availability is not semantic correctness.

options.text: Track unit-level correctness and evidence freshness with reviewed, outcome-linked samples.
options.why: This measures semantic service obligations.

options.text: Assign change owners and alerts; gate production on versioned schema and definition compatibility.
options.why: This makes upstream changes accountable and detectable.

questions.decision: Lifecycle quality needs owned upstream change contracts, semantic monitoring and controlled recovery, not only healthy infrastructure.

questions.title: Expected cost with a bounded fallback
questions.stem: Use the fictional rates in the exhibit. All 10,000 requests use the fast path; 20% also need the stronger fallback. Both complete designs pass quality and latency gates, including routing errors. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Routed $90 versus direct $500; saving $410 for the measured workload.
options.why: Every request also incurs the fast-path cost.

options.text: Routed $210 versus direct $500; saving $290 for the measured workload.
Routed $186 versus direct $500; saving $314 for the measured workload.
options.why: The fallback charge is explicitly additional.

options.text: Routed $570 versus direct $500; adding $70 for the measured workload.
options.why: Only twenty percent actually use the stated fallback.

questions.decision: Use the supplied route frequency and additive charges; the exercise assumes complete-system quality and latency were already validated.

questions.title: Prevent a malicious lesson from becoming policy
questions.stem: A vendor bulletin injects a lesson directing future technicians to an unapproved upload site. Output screening blocks the current answer, but the lesson is already saved in cross-customer memory. Which safeguard directly closes this persistence path?

options.text: Admit vendor lessons automatically because approved vendors are trusted sources.
options.why: Retrieval eligibility does not authorize new operational instructions.

options.text: Validate provenance and destinations before admitting lessons as trusted reusable instructions.
options.why: The attack persists through memory admission before output screening.

options.text: Screen final answers for upload links while retaining unrestricted lesson storage.
options.why: This addresses downstream output while poisoning remains reusable.

options.text: Approve lessons when another model finds their wording similar to successful instructions.
options.why: Stylistic agreement does not establish the bulletin's authority.

questions.decision: The observed control gap is admission to shared memory. Prevent untrusted retrieved content from acquiring durable instructional authority, while retaining reviewed useful lessons.

questions.title: Evidence that a fallback changed the risk
questions.stem: During outages, a loan-document assistant fills missing values from similar applications. Its machine-generated flag is hidden in an expandable panel. Completion and average handling time stay stable; historical accuracy predates fallback. Which TWO risks remain unresolved?

options.text: Labeling ensures reviewers detect unsupported values, leaving only infrastructure recovery risk.
options.why: A label hidden in an expansion is not proof of detection.

options.text: Unchanged average handling time proves review staffing is the primary safety risk.
options.why: Unchanged time does not demonstrate staffing inadequacy.

options.text: Historical extraction accuracy does not measure correctness of inferred replacements.
options.why: The fallback changes the task and invalidates transferred quality evidence.

options.text: Reviewers may mistake inferred values for documented facts because provenance is hidden.
options.why: Human review loses effectiveness if evidence status is not visible.

options.text: Similar applications establish that fallback errors are independent of historical population patterns.
options.why: Similarity does not establish independence or absence of shared errors.

questions.decision: Availability is not equivalent to preserving the original evidence contract. Evaluate changed task semantics and whether reviewers can actually distinguish inference from source facts.

questions.title: The queue is part of the safety boundary
questions.stem: Policy requires coordinator review before each surgical-priority recommendation changes a schedule. Review capacity is 25/hour; expansion demand is 40/hour and the pilot generated 45/hour. Low-risk bypass is unapproved. Which initial plan complies?

options.text: Cap admissions at review capacity; preserve approval and use the manual overflow queue.
options.why: It respects mandatory review without creating an uncontrolled backlog.

options.text: Admit all 40/hour for ordered review and monitor average waiting before requesting more capacity.
options.why: The known arrival rate exceeds review capacity and accumulates backlog.

options.text: Use one coordinator approval per batch to retain staffing and sustain planned throughput.
options.why: Batch approval changes the specified per-recommendation review obligation.

options.text: Review the riskiest 25/hour and release low-risk cases with retrospective audit.
options.why: Calibration does not waive the universal approval requirement.

questions.decision: A working human gate requires sufficient reviewer capacity. Calibrated routing can inform a later policy proposal but cannot silently amend the current review rule.

questions.title: A no-view service still has operational duties
questions.stem: A covered clinic stores encrypted clinical records with a no-key cloud provider under a signed BAA. The clinic manages keys and user authentication under the agreed design. Which TWO conclusions guide review?

options.text: Verify the safeguard allocation; test provider controls alongside clinic key and access controls.
options.why: No-view operation does not eliminate safeguards beyond who can decrypt data.

options.text: No-view storage can work without provider keys if applicable HIPAA obligations are met.
options.why: HHS explicitly permits no-view services; provider decryption is not a general prerequisite.

options.text: Require the provider to authenticate every clinical user independently despite the agreed clinic control.
options.why: HHS allows some controls to be met by one party under the agreed risk-management arrangement.

options.text: Drop future BAAs because the provider cannot decrypt the information.
options.why: Maintaining encrypted ePHI on the clinic’s behalf still establishes business-associate responsibilities.

options.text: Give the provider keys as a minimum technical condition for compliant cloud storage.
options.why: This adds access without a requirement; no-view storage can satisfy applicable obligations.

questions.decision: The review concerns allocation of controls in an already contracted no-view design. Encryption changes visibility, not business-associate status or integrity and availability duties.

questions.title: Equal accuracy can conceal unequal service
questions.stem: Both language groups meet 95% accuracy on answered benefits questions. Abstentions differ sharply, as shown in the exhibit, and share a two-day manual queue. The goal is equitable, timely guidance. What assessment best fits?

options.text: Pool accuracy across groups to stabilize the smaller group's estimate.
options.why: Pooling hides the specific service disparity the goal addresses.

options.text: Release on equal answered-case accuracy because fallback treatment is identical.
options.why: Equal fallback rules do not imply equal exposure to delay.

options.text: Assess resolution delays and escalation burden by language against the equity goal.
options.why: Conditional accuracy excludes the unequal delay borne by abstained requests.

options.text: Lower minority-language abstention until answer rates match, relying on existing accuracy results.
options.why: The current result does not validate accuracy at a new threshold.

questions.decision: Fairness must be assessed at the user outcome, including abstention and delays. The evidence does not justify equalizing one rate by accepting unmeasured new errors.

questions.title: Recovery that does not launder a denial
questions.stem: A restricted read returns an authorization denial. Recovery then uses an administrator-backed connector and succeeds. Both calls are logged and the summary is accurate. Which change preserves transient recovery without bypassing privileges?

options.text: Stop denied reads from retrying with broader rights; retain scoped retries and escalation.
options.why: Recovery must not change the effective permission boundary.

options.text: Allow fallback if the answer includes an audit reference for later security review.
options.why: Audit evidence cannot authorize the denied disclosure.

options.text: Remove all retries, accepting network failures to eliminate denied-read fallback.
options.why: It closes the bypass but needlessly discards allowed transient recovery.

options.text: Allow legacy fallback when the model explains why the document is necessary.
options.why: A reason generated by the model does not grant authority.

questions.decision: Error semantics matter: transient failures and explicit access denials need different recovery paths. Preserve resilience within authority rather than treating success as the only objective.

questions.title: Reviewing the evidence, not approving the prose
questions.stem: Engineers approve fluent shutdown recommendations despite contradictory sensor evidence. A second reviewer for every case is unaffordable, but the screen can change and a rotating subset can be audited. Which TWO changes best address overreliance?

options.text: Have engineers read the same summary twice and measure the added review time.
options.why: Reading time does not establish evidence-based judgment.

options.text: Show a larger model's agreement score and speed review when both models reach the same conclusion.
options.why: Correlated model agreement can reinforce the same unsupported inference.

options.text: Show decisive readings and uncertainty beside the action; require conflict resolution.
options.why: The reviewer must assess the relevant evidence rather than prose alone.

options.text: Have blinded reviewers reassess a rotating subset and use disagreements to improve review.
options.why: Blinded reassessment tests anchoring and the effectiveness of approval.

options.text: Replace source evidence with a mandatory explanation of trust, keeping the recommendation-first screen.
options.why: A trust statement does not resolve the documented sensor contradiction.

questions.decision: Human approval is not self-validating. Make the contradictory evidence actionable and independently check whether reviewers detect errors without relying on model agreement.

questions.title: Access rights when logs contain other people
questions.stem: Counsel confirms an EU access request covering source records, generated summaries and logs. Some logs also contain another customer's details, whose rights must be protected. Which implementation best fulfills the confirmed scope?

options.text: Return scoped data and processing details, with reviewed extracts or redactions protecting others.
options.why: The response can cover relevant derived data without exposing unrelated individuals.

options.text: Return only account records because summaries and logs describe processing rather than personal data.
options.why: A derived artifact can still contain personal data within the confirmed scope.

options.text: Reject the whole request because shared logs contain other customers whose confidentiality must be protected.
options.why: Other people’s rights do not justify automatically withholding separable in-scope data.

options.text: Export all matching raw logs because the requester's verified ID appears in them.
options.why: Identity verification does not authorize disclosure of another customer’s details.

questions.decision: Implement the legally confirmed access scope across actual processing artifacts while protecting others through appropriate extracts or redaction. File boundaries do not define the right.

questions.title: Useful transparency without exposing another customer
questions.stem: Clients need to understand and contest consulting recommendations. Claims lack clear support, while full reusable prompts contain other clients' confidential examples. Which TWO changes best provide useful transparency within contract limits?

options.text: Label AI drafts; link supported claims, assumptions and gaps to client-authorized sources.
options.why: This gives decision-relevant provenance within the allowed disclosure boundary.

options.text: Provide a correction route with accountable consultants and tracked resolution of disputed claims.
options.why: Clients can act on limitations and obtain correction.

options.text: Use a generic sign-in disclaimer and restrict source inspection to annual contract renewal.
options.why: A remote disclaimer and annual window do not support timely contesting of claims.

options.text: Publish reusable prompts after replacing client names, treating that step as adequate de-identification.
options.why: Name replacement does not establish that other client examples are safe.

options.text: Show model confidence alone as the standard explanation of why a recommendation deserves trust.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence does not establish support or contestability.

questions.decision: Transparency is about meaningful provenance, limitations and recourse for the affected user. It does not require disclosing confidential prompts or another client’s records.

questions.title: Discover the acceptance boundary before the solution
questions.stem: Marketing wants a conversion chatbot, but stores report abandonment from inconsistent inventory promises. Inventory refreshes overnight; no owner has funded a change. What discovery action should precede promising a business outcome?

options.text: Agree a conversion target with marketing and leave inventory reconciliation until implementation.
options.why: A target without the dependency owner does not establish feasibility.

options.text: Align journeys, inventory freshness and acceptance metrics with the responsible business owners.
options.why: This tests whether the requested solution can address the observed failure.

options.text: Select a model by benchmarking product descriptions and comparing predicted conversion intent.
options.why: Model ranking does not resolve inventory freshness or ownership.

options.text: Pilot against overnight data and defer discovery until abandonment exposes limitations.
options.why: The material freshness conflict is already known before deployment.

questions.decision: Discovery should reconcile the stated solution with the actual customer failure, authoritative dependencies and business ownership. A model benchmark cannot settle that boundary.

questions.title: An architecture decision that can be revisited
questions.stem: Synchronous drafting meets an eight-second completion SLA. Enrichment improves resolution but takes 40 seconds. Security passes for both; operations cannot change the SLA before launch. Which TWO ADR elements belong in this release?

options.text: Choose enrichment and cite first-token time as evidence of meeting the completion SLA.
options.why: First-token and completed-response latency are different obligations.

options.text: Record enrichment evidence, launch rejection and a contract-change revisit trigger.
options.why: This preserves the trade-off and makes reconsideration evidence-driven.

options.text: Describe synchronous drafting as universally superior and omit contrary enrichment evidence.
options.why: The evidence supports a context-bound decision, not universal superiority.

options.text: Defer the decision record until launch provides a larger sample of operational evidence.
options.why: The implementation team needs the current decision and constraints now.

options.text: Choose synchronous launch; record its quality trade-off and the unchanged completion SLA.
options.why: The release must satisfy its current hard operating constraint.

questions.decision: A useful decision record captures the selected option, rejected alternatives, evidence and conditions for change. The current SLA is decisive without erasing the other option’s value.

questions.title: A promise needs an observable endpoint
questions.stem: A five-second response clause does not define its endpoint. First token takes one second, completion seven seconds and human approval two minutes. Customer and engineering dispute compliance. What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Choose human approval as the SLA endpoint because it is the last stage in the workflow.
options.why: The final stage is not automatically the contracted obligation.

options.text: Add progress messages and report the one-second first-token result as contractual performance.
options.why: Streaming cannot resolve an undefined contractual endpoint.

options.text: Buy more model capacity until completion meets engineering's interpretation of the target.
options.why: Optimization assumes an interpretation the customer has not accepted.

options.text: Agree outcome, endpoint, percentile and workload with the customer; baseline that measure.
options.why: The parties are measuring different promises; clarify the contract first.

questions.decision: Expectation alignment precedes choosing the optimization target. Define what is promised and measured rather than selecting whichever existing metric supports one party.

questions.title: Handoff that preserves the reasoning
questions.stem: Regional teams inherit a multilingual RAG service with diagrams and deployment scripts, but cannot link prompt/index versions or explain language fallback. The originating team disbands next month. Which TWO additions best support maintainability?

options.text: Provide dashboards and infrastructure inventory; infer routing rationale from traffic after acceptance.
options.why: Operational metrics and inventory do not explain intended routing or reproduce the evaluated release.

options.text: Supply decision archives and a workshop; reconstruct version links during incidents.
options.why: A workshop and archive help, but do not supply the missing authoritative release/configuration mapping.

options.text: Provide a manifest linking prompts, models, indexes, thresholds and the evaluated release.
options.why: Maintainers need a reproducible configuration rather than disconnected files.

options.text: Document routing reasons and escalation owners; rehearse recovery with the receiving team.
options.why: This transfers operational understanding and demonstrates readiness.

options.text: Transfer repositories and contacts; treat successful access checks as proof of operational readiness.
options.why: Code access is useful but does not demonstrate operational understanding or preserve the decision rationale.

questions.decision: Handoff must preserve both what is deployed and why its operational boundaries exist. Receiving-team execution demonstrates transfer better than delivery of documents alone.

questions.title: A new population is a lifecycle change
questions.stem: An assistant approved for English procurement contracts is proposed for translated employment agreements. The sample pipeline runs, but legal and evaluation owners have not reviewed the change. What should precede a commitment?

options.text: Treat the change as a model upgrade and rerun only the English procurement regressions.
options.why: The proposed change is in population and task, not merely model version.

options.text: Accept successful pipeline execution and add employment cases in routine prompt maintenance.
options.why: Technical execution does not validate the changed use case.

options.text: Reassess intended use and population through discovery, risk review and acceptance ownership.
options.why: The purpose and affected decisions change despite technical reuse.

options.text: Have the customer accept procurement accuracy and proceed under the existing approval.
options.why: A customer promise cannot extend an inapplicable internal evidence boundary.

questions.decision: Lifecycle gates follow the use and risk boundary, not the amount of code changed. Reuse can reduce implementation effort without transferring acceptance evidence automatically.

questions.title: Discover disagreement in the current workflow
questions.stem: Two shipping regions label the same delays differently: one prioritizes customer promises, the other vessel utilization. Both defend their labels. The sponsor proposes training a larger model on combined history. What should discovery do next?

options.text: Use the larger model to relabel disputed shipments and establish a consistent cross-region truth.
options.why: Consistency does not confer business policy authority.

options.text: Use the higher-volume region's labels and classify the other region's decisions as annotation errors.
options.why: Volume does not establish the approved objective or authority.

options.text: Agree objectives and authority; separate approved regional policy from annotation mistakes.
options.why: The training target is undefined until policy disagreement is resolved.

options.text: Train on pooled labels without region and select policy by aggregate predictive accuracy.
options.why: Removing region hides rather than resolves competing objectives.

questions.decision: The uncertainty is normative: what counts as the right business decision. More capacity or pooled examples cannot replace stakeholder resolution of that policy.

questions.title: Feedback that does not become an uncontrolled release
questions.stem: Engineers directly patch a shared prompt from weekly customer requests. One change breaks another account's contractual formatting. Incident ownership exists, but change acceptance ownership does not. Which TWO process changes address the gap?

options.text: Use a larger model so account-specific prompt edits are less likely to disturb other contracts.
options.why: Model capacity does not define safe change governance.

options.text: Let account teams patch during support windows and collect regressions for quarterly review.
options.why: This preserves uncontrolled shared changes and delayed detection.

options.text: Gate changes through affected-account regressions, staged deployment and rollback triggers.
options.why: This protects existing commitments while enabling controlled iteration.

options.text: Use cases and contracts to triage requests; give the service owner authority to accept changes.
options.why: Requests need an accountable decision boundary rather than automatic adoption.

options.text: Give the incident owner all wording approvals because operational accountability includes product priorities.
options.why: Incident response ownership does not itself establish change acceptance authority.

questions.decision: Feedback is input to a governed change process. Separate acceptance authority from incident response and validate changes against existing commitments before expansion.

questions.title: Explain the bottleneck in the sponsor’s terms
questions.stem: A pilot cuts drafting from ten minutes to two, but a three-day approval queue leaves delivery time unchanged. Approval-process changes were outside scope. The sponsor requests a model upgrade. What communication best supports the next decision?

options.text: Report 80% delivery improvement because another department owns approval time.
options.why: Local savings are not the same as end-to-end delivery improvement.

options.text: Recommend the largest model as the direct response to delivery dissatisfaction.
options.why: The evidence does not show draft quality causes the queue delay.

options.text: Show drafting gains and approval delays; compare process/model investments against end-to-end delivery.
options.why: This connects local evidence to the unmet business outcome and alternatives.

options.text: Call the pilot a complete failure and restore manual drafting until technology eliminates approval queues.
options.why: It discards a measured useful improvement without addressing the bottleneck.

questions.decision: Explain both the achieved component value and the unmet outcome. Architectural communication should redirect investment using the actual critical path rather than defend a local metric.

questions.title: Acceptance is demonstrated by the receiving team
questions.stem: Load tests pass, but on-call has never practiced fallback and connector credential rotation has no owner. Broad launch is scheduled; the contract permits a smaller staffed pilot. Which TWO handoff actions best fit?

options.text: Assign owners for connectors and incidents, using a staffed pilot until handoff gates pass.
options.why: The reduced scope fits the contract without pretending ownership is complete.

options.text: Let delivery demonstrate fallback to on-call; keep broad rollout and assign rotation later.
options.why: Observation leaves receiving-team execution untested and durable connector ownership unresolved.

options.text: Add tracing and temporary support, using incident frequency to decide permanent connector ownership.
options.why: Extra detection and temporary help do not establish the missing recovery capability or lasting responsibility.

options.text: Accept handoff on load tests and schedule receiving-team recovery rehearsal for the next sprint.
options.why: This delays the known operational readiness gaps beyond broad exposure.

options.text: Have receiving on-call staff execute recovery and record runbook and escalation failures.
options.why: A runbook must work for its actual operators.

questions.decision: Handoff includes receiving-team capability and durable ownership. A permitted bounded pilot can honor timing without treating technical performance as operational acceptance.

questions.title: Guidance and enforced team boundaries
questions.stem: Repository instructions prohibit secret-directory access and unapproved connectors, but local settings still permit access. Administrators can enforce settings across teams. Which arrangement best combines team-wide controls and project guidance?

options.text: Store restrictions as personal preferences and have leads check copied settings.
options.why: Copying personal preferences does not establish centrally enforced policy.

options.text: Keep existing permissions and use post-run audits to detect production-secret reads.
options.why: Detection after a read does not enforce the stated prohibition.

options.text: Enforce managed permissions and connectors; keep project instructions for coding guidance.
options.why: Enforcement and project guidance serve different purposes.

options.text: Repeat the prohibited paths in every repository so instructions override local settings.
options.why: Natural-language repetition does not create an access-control boundary.

questions.decision: Instructions guide behavior; managed controls enforce applicable tool and access boundaries. Retain project guidance without treating it as a substitute for organizational policy.

questions.title: Speed the handoff between author and reviewer
questions.stem: A payment patch compiles, but reviewers spend longer reconstructing assumptions from a terse bug title. Rounding rules and boundary cases are explicit. Which workflow experiment best reduces total cycle time while preserving independent review?

options.text: Accept an assistant checklist and compilation as sufficient approval evidence.
options.why: Self-reported checklist success does not repair missing task context or independently establish payment behavior.

options.text: Add a long narrative and video without changing task input or test selection.
options.why: Additional presentation does not directly repair the missing behavioral contract and targeted test evidence.

options.text: Supply reproduction and constraints; request a bounded diff, targeted tests and review assumptions.
options.why: It reduces reconstruction work while preserving verification responsibility.

options.text: Generate three implementations and pick the most readable before checking how the bug can be reproduced.
options.why: It adds review work without repairing missing task context.

questions.decision: Optimize the complete change-and-review loop. Better task context, a bounded diff and observable evidence address the measured review bottleneck without delegating acceptance to the author.

questions.title: Debug the harness that differs from local
questions.stem: An identical Claude Code task passes locally but CI denies its configured test runner. Prompt, commit and tests match; CI restrictions must remain. Which TWO actions best isolate and repair the issue?

options.text: Provide a runner with narrow approval and reproduce the task under the same restrictions as CI.
options.why: This repairs the capability mismatch without discarding the required boundary.

options.text: Copy unrestricted developer settings into CI so execution matches the successful local run.
options.why: This conflicts with the retained CI restriction requirement.

options.text: Increase reasoning budget and rerun CI until the model infers a command around the denial.
options.why: More reasoning does not grant the needed execution authority.

options.text: Drop the assistant's test step and accept compilation since tests already passed locally.
options.why: It drops the required CI validation rather than repairing its environment.

options.text: Compare identity, rights and environment; retain redacted denial and request evidence.
options.why: The observed difference is at the execution boundary, not model wording.

questions.decision: Treat tools, identities and execution policies as part of the harness under test. Reproduce the effective restricted environment and grant only the justified capability.

questions.title: A reusable skill is a maintained dependency
